title: Medieval close: a mirror
hookLine: every age of saints shows what that age most needed

cards: Hold up a mirror to a room and it shows you the room. Not an idea of it: what's actually there, including what's missing, the empty chair, the bare wall.
For a long stretch, this path has walked through the middle ages, from a monastery bell to a stripped abbey roof. Today, hold up a mirror to the whole stretch. The mirror is the saints.

teach.b: Here's one way to read them: each age's saints show what that age was short of. First, violence.
In an age of private wars and crusades, you met the Peace of God, Louis the king doing justice under an oak, and Francis walking unarmed to a sultan. Peace was what was missing, so peacemakers shone.
Second, ignorance and confusion. The universities rose, Thomas the dumb ox reasoned his way toward God, and Bonaventure mapped a journey of the mind.
When the popes lived away from Rome, a dyer's daughter, Catherine, told one to go home. Third, suffering.
When plague came, Julian, walled in beside her church, heard that all shall be well, and saw all that is made, as small as a hazelnut in her hand. Elizabeth and Catherine of Genoa nursed the sick.

teach.h: AN AGE OF GREED: THOSE WHO CHANGED.

teach.b: When popes grew worldly and empires reached for gold, Las Casas changed, a pope wrote that the peoples of the Americas are truly human, Juan Diego the little one carried flowers to a bishop, and Fisher refused a king.
Mirrors don't flatter. Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face."
Looking back, you see these centuries through a glass too: partly, darkly, with your own reflection in the frame.
And Jesus told some questioners who could read the sky that they could not read "the signs of the times." That's the harder question this block leaves behind. Not what did their age need.

how: Catholics read the lives of the saints through the year, keeping their feasts in the Church's calendar; homilies and spiritual reading often ask what a saint's life says to the present day.

a perfect age with nothing missing.
games.why: peacemakers in violent times, teachers in confused ones, healers in plague, people who changed in an age of greed, and the harder question: what does ours need?

practice: Look around your own time the way you've looked at theirs: your city, your news, your group chats, your family.

Ask quietly what is missing here, and what kind of person would shine simply by being the opposite of what's wrong; don't rush, let one answer come. If you pray, ask to be shown it; if you don't, just keep the question open.
